query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings, wear resistance is governed by a dynamic amorphization process that transforms the initially coarse-grained surface into an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer via inverse Hall-Petch behavior, thus reducing shear strength and friction during wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A HEA protective coating with a coarse- to moderately-grained microstructure (e.g., the typical state of CoCrFeMnNi alloys before significant wear)
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to controlled wear tests in an inert (ultra-high vacuum) environment, and in a separate set, inhibit dynamic amorphization by introducing a dopant or employing a thermal treatment that stabilizes the grain boundaries against refinement.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted in an inert atmosphere (to minimize oxidation) under controlled mechanical loading that promotes grain refinement processes; comparison between a standard sample and one modified to resist dynamic amorphization.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer (resulting from dynamic amorphization)
generation.mechanism: Under wear-induced stress, the HEA undergoes a transformation where dynamic amorphization leads to significant grain refinement (inverse Hall-Petch behavior), which in turn reduces shear strength and friction. This process results in lower friction coefficients (~0.3) and exceptionally low wear rates (~10⁻⁶ mm³/N-m) by facilitating superplasticity in the deformed layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: The baseline (untreated) sample should develop an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer, exhibit low friction and wear rates. By contrast, samples treated to suppress dynamic amorphization should show higher friction and increased wear, as the protective layer will be diminished or absent.
generation.baseline: Performance of HEA coatings under inert wear testing without any modification to hinder grain refinement and dynamic amorphization.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA protective coatings in environments where oxidation is minimized (e.g., ultra-high vacuum) and sufficient mechanical energy is delivered to trigger grain refinement. Its applicability in ambient or oxidizing conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The degree to which sample composition variations or environmental factors (such as slight oxidation even under inert conditions) might affect the dynamic amorphization process is uncertain, as is the precise quantitative impact of the intervention on friction and wear metrics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi). One set remains untreated (baseline) while the other set is modified – either through doping with a grain-boundary stabilizer or via a thermal process – to inhibit dynamic amorphization. Expose both sets to identical wear tests in an ultra-high vacuum environment. Post-test, use STEM to characterize the near-surface grain structure and perform friction and wear rate measurements.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during wear tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both modified and baseline samples develop similar ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layers and exhibit comparable low friction and wear rates, this would falsify the hypothesis that the dynamic amorphization process (and related inverse Hall-Petch effect) governs the improved wear performance.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
